chapters.1.lds: The selected lesson teaches unity in Christ’s Church. Why does Paul answer competing party names with questions about baptism and crucifixion?
chapters.1.summary: Paul and Sosthenes write to the assembly of God at Corinth. Paul thanks God for their gifts of speech and knowledge. Then he begs them to agree, for Chloe’s people report quarrels. Some say they follow Paul, and others Apollos, Cephas, or Christ. Paul is glad he baptized only a few of them. He says the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing. Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but he announces Christ crucified. God chose the weak and lowly, so no one may boast.
chapters.2.lds: The selected lesson teaches reliance on God’s wisdom. Why does Paul recall his fear rather than present an impressive speaking record?
chapters.2.summary: Paul recalls his first visit to Corinth. He did not come with fine speech or wisdom. He decided to know nothing among them but Jesus Christ crucified. He was weak, afraid, and trembling. Yet he says there is a wisdom for the mature, hidden and now revealed. The rulers of this age did not know it and crucified the Lord. God’s Spirit reveals what God has given. The natural person does not receive these things, but “we have Christ’s mind.”
chapters.3.lds: The selected lesson uses God’s building to teach shared work and unity. How do planting and watering differ from giving growth?
chapters.3.summary: Paul says he fed the Corinthians milk, because they were not ready for solid food. Their jealousy and quarrels show they are still fleshly. Paul and Apollos are only servants. One planted and one watered, but God gave the growth. Paul laid a foundation, which is Jesus Christ, and others build on it. Fire will test each builder’s work. The believers are God’s temple, and God’s Spirit lives in them. So no one should boast in men, for all things are theirs.
chapters.4.lds: What does the question about received gifts expose in the hearers’ boasting?
chapters.4.summary: Paul calls himself a servant of Christ and a steward of God’s mysteries. A steward must be faithful, and the Lord is the judge. He tells them not to be puffed up for one teacher against another. He says they act as if they already reign as kings. The apostles, he says, are like men sentenced to death. They are hungry, beaten, homeless, and treated as the world’s filth. Paul writes as a father to warn his children. He is sending Timothy and plans to come himself.
chapters.5.lds: Why does Paul distinguish the group’s own boundary from judgment outside?
chapters.5.summary: Paul has heard that a man in the assembly lives with his father’s wife. He says even the Gentiles do not accept this. The assembly is proud when it should mourn. Paul tells them to gather and remove the man. A little yeast leavens the whole lump, and Christ is their Passover. He explains an earlier letter. He did not mean to avoid immoral people of the world. He meant one called a brother who lives that way.
chapters.6.lds: The selected lesson teaches that physical bodies are sacred. How can an action claimed as freedom become a source of control?
chapters.6.summary: Paul rebukes believers who take one another to court before unbelievers. He asks if no one among them is wise enough to decide. It would be better to be wronged. He lists those who will not inherit God’s kingdom. He says some of them were such, but they were washed and made holy. Then he answers the saying that all things are lawful. The body is for the Lord and will be raised. It is a temple of the Holy Spirit, bought with a price.
chapters.7.lds: Why does Paul distinguish commands from his own judgment about unmarried life?
chapters.7.summary: Paul answers questions the Corinthians wrote to him about marriage. Husband and wife owe each other their bodies. The married should not separate, and he says this command is the Lord’s. A believer should stay with an unbelieving spouse who is willing. Each should remain in the state in which he was called. About the unmarried, Paul gives his own judgment. Because of the present distress it is good to remain as they are. Yet one who marries does not sin.
chapters.8.lds: How does the observer’s conscience change the confident believer’s food choice?
chapters.8.summary: Paul turns to food sacrificed to idols. He says knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. An idol is nothing, and there is one God and one Lord. Not everyone has that knowledge. Some still think of the idol when they eat, and their conscience suffers. Food does not bring anyone nearer to God. A weak believer may see another eat in an idol’s temple and follow. Paul says he would never eat meat if it made a brother stumble.
chapters.9.lds: The selected lesson cites Paul’s instruction about support for gospel teachers. Why does Paul defend a right that he chooses not to use?
chapters.9.summary: Paul asks if he is not free and an apostle. He says he has the right to food, drink, and support. A soldier, a vinedresser, and a shepherd all live from their work. The law says not to muzzle an ox that treads grain. Yet Paul has not used this right. He offers the good news free of charge. He becomes as a Jew to Jews and weak to the weak. He trains like a runner so that he is not disqualified.
chapters.10.lds: The selected lesson teaches escape from temptation and unity through the sacrament. Why does an explicit notice about food change the invited meal?
chapters.10.summary: Paul recalls Israel in the wilderness. All passed through the sea and ate the same spiritual food, yet most fell. These things are examples and warnings. God will not let them be tempted beyond their strength. Paul tells them to flee idolatry. They cannot share the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Meat from the market may be eaten without questions. If someone says it was offered to idols, they should not eat.
chapters.11.lds: The selected lesson connects self examination and the sacrament with unity. How does waiting for others answer the shame caused by unequal eating?
chapters.11.summary: Paul gives instructions about head coverings when men and women pray or prophesy. He then turns to their shared meal and does not praise them. There are divisions when they meet. Each eats his own supper first, so one is hungry and another is drunk. Paul repeats what he received about the Lord’s bread and cup. Whoever eats in an unworthy way is guilty concerning the Lord’s body and blood. Each should examine himself. When they come together to eat, they should wait for one another.
chapters.12.lds: The selected lesson teaches using spiritual gifts to help others. Why does the body give greater honor to apparently weaker members?
chapters.12.summary: Paul writes about spiritual gifts. There are different gifts, services, and workings, but the same Spirit, Lord, and God. Each receives a gift for the good of all. Paul lists wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, languages, and more. He compares the assembly to one body with many members. A foot cannot say it does not belong, and an eye cannot dismiss a hand. If one member suffers, all suffer. God has set apostles, prophets, teachers, and others in the assembly.
chapters.13.lds: The selected lesson teaches charity as the greatest spiritual gift. How does love answer the earlier jealousy and boasting?
chapters.13.summary: Paul says languages of men and angels are noise without love. Prophecy, knowledge, and faith that moves mountains are nothing without it. Giving away everything gains nothing without it. He then says what love does. It is patient and kind, and it does not envy, brag, or seek its own. It bears, believes, hopes, and endures all things. Prophecy, languages, and knowledge will end, but love never fails. Faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest is love.
chapters.14.lds: The selected lessons teach using gifts to support the gathered church. Why do interpreters and taking turns matter for the gathered group?
chapters.14.summary: Paul tells them to follow love and to desire prophecy most. One who speaks in another language speaks to God, and no one understands. One who prophesies builds up the assembly. A trumpet with an unclear sound calls no one to battle. Paul would rather speak five words with understanding than ten thousand in another language. At most two or three should speak in another language, with an interpreter. Prophets should speak in turn while others weigh it. God is a God of peace, and all should be done in order.
chapters.15.lds: The selected lesson teaches universal resurrection and connects baptism for the dead with temple service. These later Church practices remain distinct from Paul’s brief reference. Doctrine and Covenants 128:16 quotes verse 29. How does future resurrection give meaning to present labor?
chapters.15.summary: Paul repeats the good news he delivered. Christ died for sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day. He appeared to Cephas, the twelve, five hundred others, James, and Paul. Some in Corinth say there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul says that if so, Christ was not raised and faith is empty. But Christ has been raised, the first fruit of those who sleep. The body is sown perishable and raised imperishable, like a seed. Death is swallowed up, so their labor is not in vain.
chapters.16.lds: Why should the believers approve the people carrying their gift?
chapters.16.summary: Paul gives directions for the collection for the saints. Each should set money aside on the first day of the week. Approved people will carry the gift to Jerusalem. Paul plans to come through Macedonia and stay in Ephesus until Pentecost. He asks them to receive Timothy without fear and says Apollos will come later. He tells them to watch, stand firm, and do everything in love. He commends the household of Stephanas. He signs the greeting with his own hand.
